title: Systematic review with meta‐analysis: the gastrointestinal benefits of <scp>COX</scp>‐2 selective inhibitors with concomitant use of low‐dose aspirin

sections.abstract: <jats:title>Summary</jats:title><jats:sec><jats:title>Background</jats:title><jats:p>It is uncertain whether concurrent use of low‐dose aspirin removes the gastrointestinal benefit displayed by <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">COX</jats:styled-content>‐2 selective inhibitors (coxibs) when compared to traditional nonsteroidal anti‐inflammatory drugs (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">NSAID</jats:styled-content>s).</jats:p></jats:sec><jats:sec><jats:title>Aim</jats:title><jats:p>To evaluate the gastrointestinal risks associated with coxibs and traditional <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">NSAID</jats:styled-content>s and the interaction with concurrent use of low‐dose aspirin.</jats:p></jats:sec><jats:sec><jats:title>Methods</jats:title><jats:p>We searched <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">MEDLINE</jats:styled-content>,<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case"> EMBASE</jats:styled-content> and the Cochrane Library through April 2016 to identify randomised trials comparing the gastrointestinal risk between coxibs and traditional <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">NSAID</jats:styled-content>s in patients taking or not taking low‐dose aspirin. Results were combined using random effects meta‐analysis. Subgroup analyses by concurrent use of aspirin were undertaken.</jats:p></jats:sec><jats:sec><jats:title>Results</jats:title><jats:p>Eleven trials (84 150 participants) were included. The overall relative risk (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">RR</jats:styled-content>) of coxibs vs. traditional <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">NSAID</jats:styled-content>s for complicated gastrointestinal events was 0.54 (95% CI, confidence interval 0.32–0.92), with a significant subgroup difference (<jats:italic>P</jats:italic> = 0.04) according to concurrent use of aspirin (used: <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">RR</jats:styled-content> = 0.96, 95% <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">CI</jats:styled-content> 0.66–1.24; not used: <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">RR</jats:styled-content> = 0.33, 95% <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">CI</jats:styled-content> 0.14–0.83). The overall <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">RR</jats:styled-content> for clinical gastrointestinal events was 0.59 (95% <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">CI</jats:styled-content> 0.47–0.75), with a significant subgroup difference according to aspirin usage (<jats:italic>P</jats:italic> = 0.008; used: <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">RR</jats:styled-content> = 0.77, 95% <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">CI</jats:styled-content> 0.62–0.95; not used: <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">RR</jats:styled-content> = 0.50, 95% <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">CI</jats:styled-content> 0.39–0.64). Overall coxibs were associated with significantly lower risk of symptomatic ulcers (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">RR</jats:styled-content> = 0.60, 95% <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">CI</jats:styled-content> 0.50–0.72) and endoscopic ulcers (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">RR</jats:styled-content> = 0.29, 95% <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">CI</jats:styled-content> 0.16–0.53) than traditional <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">NSAID</jats:styled-content>s; a significant subgroup difference was shown for endoscopic ulcers (<jats:italic>P</jats:italic> = 0.05) but not for symptomatic ulcers (<jats:italic>P</jats:italic> = 0.27).</jats:p></jats:sec><jats:sec><jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title><jats:p>Concomitant use of low‐dose aspirin reduces but does not completely eliminate the gastrointestinal benefit of coxibs over traditional <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">NSAID</jats:styled-content>s.</jats:p></jats:sec>
